#1723. O'Neill hits out at critics as Celtic boss issues surprising response to McGregor's midweek comments

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 15:03 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 15:30 EDT, 30 October 2026

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill has claimed some of the club’s critics are only seeking to cause division within the camp.

On the back of a 2-2 draw with Dundee United earlier this week, Celtic skipper Callum McGregor claimed they are playing like a basketball team who lack control in matches.

McGregor also appeared to question the fact that Celtic started the match effectively with three strikers across the frontline in Kasper Hogh, Camilo Duran and Callum Osmand.

‘It’s not really having a nailed-on profile for each of the positions,’ said McGregor. ‘The players behave like a winger, or they behave like a striker.

‘You can get away with it for a few games but if it’s a striker playing as a winger, you are going to get that behaviour a lot of the time.

‘You’ve got enough quality so you can score goals and get away with it. But we have to try to get the team functioning the way it should.

O'Neill is satisfied with Celtic's start to the season despite criticism over performances

‘Then that will alleviate all the other problems that we are encountering, where it becomes a bit like basketball, you lose control and spend the next 15 minutes trying to get possession back.’

At half-time in the game against United at Parkhead, O’Neill took Hogh off and reverted to a more traditional system with Jota and Haissem Hassan coming on as wingers to replace the misfiring Dane and Osmand.

Celtic eventually fought back to claim a point, but McGregor’s comments became the subject of much scrutiny.

It is not the first time a senior player has spoken out this season, with Cameron Carter-Vickers claiming that Celtic’s style of play was ‘random’ after the Old Firm defeats to Rangers.

O’Neill insists he actually agrees with McGregor’s comments — but has vowed to find a solution at the top end of the pitch.

The veteran boss also appeared to snipe back at some of the critics who have claimed that there is unrest among the squad.

‘I’ve said this to you before, I totally agree that Osmand is actually really a centre-forward,’ said O’Neill when asked about McGregor’s verdict.

‘I’ve said it at the press conference, that he is essentially a centre-forward who probably would play off somebody strong alongside him.

‘I'm not so sure that he could lead the line on his own. And that Duran is really a centre-forward.

‘So the players are getting to know each other. It’s really as simple as that. So I’m in total agreement with Callum. We’ll sort it out.

The manager admits that the likes of Camilo Duran are currently being played out of position

‘We seem to be doing okay domestically, trying to sort it out.

‘There’s a few players that haven’t had a chance. [Jordan] Lotomba hasn’t had a chance yet to play. There’ll be moments, absolutely.

‘Young [Joel] Van Den Berg has trained today. So over the course of the next number of weeks, between now and Christmas, I think everybody will be on the field of play.

‘And then it’s a matter of establishing right positions as much as possible.

‘Players have played out of position before. I don’t know whether it was a big issue when young Osmand came on in the Benfica game and set us alight.

‘I come in here [to the press conference] every single week and I’m most of the time pretty buoyed by things.

‘Don’t try and throw a lot of divides in. At the end of the day, we’re doing fine.

‘A lot of lads here didn’t even do pre-season with us. A number of players came in quite late on, so it will take time for us.

‘So we need to hang in there, and at this minute I think we’re hanging in.’

With Rangers playing Aberdeen in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup, Celtic travel to Falkirk tomorrow knowing that a victory would send them seven points clear of their Old Firm rivals.

O'Neill added: ‘I think we’ve done fine, we’re leading the league with a four-point gap at this minute, which is nothing at all at this stage of the season.

‘We fought back and retrieved those kind of leads on a couple of occasions last season.

‘We’ll try and get a result or two in European football which would be nice, but domestically we’ve been fine.

‘Falkirk had a bit of a stodgy start, but they are flying now, so we know it’ll be a difficult game for us.’

#1722. “I can’t change it” – Chivu looks back after three derby defeats to Milan

After last night’s win against Inter, AC Milan have now gone eight games without a defeat in the Derby della Madonnina.

In years gone by, the derby was a result to skip over for Milan. It was a defeat waiting to happen and it seemingly couldn’t be changed and then it flipped. Matteo Gabbia’s goal stopped the streak and in turn, it started a new one.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The Rossoneri entered last night’s game with a run of seven unbeaten and they finished the night with eight unbeaten and a fourth consecutive win. It’s a first in itself for more than 50 years, which is telling.

It’s a result which brought Gerry Cardinale to tears and it’s clear that something has really clicked at San Siro, as the player ratings showed.

Speaking at a press conference after the game, as relayed by MilanNews, the Inter coach spoke about several things, including his unfavourable record in the Derby della Madonnina.

“Compared to last year, there’s something to note about our approach to matches: the superficiality and casualness with which we handle certain situations, where we lack a bit of grit, a bit of determination, a bit of danger perception. But we need to rediscover them.

“We need to be aware that right now, despite a few more points than last year, we’ve lost something that absolutely needs to be rediscovered.”

“I couldn’t, because the forwards have had some problems in the last few days. Bonny only made himself available on the last day after two days with a fever of 39°C and severe nausea and vomiting, so we were forced to find a solution, to make a virtue of necessity, changing the system a bit.

“We knew that, in this type of match, it would be the right thing to have pace on the wings with Spence and Carlos and attack the line a bit more, as well as looking for depth in space with Diouf operating under the striker, looking for both him and Sucic between the lines.

“Unfortunately, sometimes things don’t work out, but, I repeat, we were forced to change.”

“It’s too easy to talk now that Lautaro is injured and the other two forwards aren’t feeling well. These things happen, fortunately not often. We’ll make some assessments, but we’re still happy with our four forwards, in addition to what Lavelli gives us, what Mosconi gives us, and whoever we bring in from the Under 23s.

“But, I repeat, it’s too easy to bring these things up at a time when two forwards aren’t at their best and the third is injured.”

Is there something mental that comes into play in the derby?

“There’s always something mental, I think, and history teaches us this, when you get to play another season after winning.

“So, let’s try not to throw everything away and try to rediscover some determination, some humility in doing certain things, starting with myself, because I’m primarily responsible for everything we do.

“We shouldn’t throw everything away because we’ve reached the tenth matchday and this is the first game we’ve lost. We’ve got 25 points, and last year we’d got fewer, but we’ve always been able to react, we’ve always kept our feet on the ground and our heads down to build a strong season.

“That’s what we’d like to do again this year, because we have this desire and this ambition to have another strong season; we just need to find the way to build it again.”

#1721. Arsenal 2-0 Everton: Konsa and Gabriel get the goals

Arsenal made it 7 wins from 8 so far in the Premier League this season with a relatively comfortable 2-0 win over Everton at home yesterday.

Mikel Arteta made some changes from the midweek team, with Ben White, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres all handed starts. And as a team that has been a bit slow to get going in games so far, an early goal was just the tonic after all the effort against Bayern Munich on Wednesday.

We put pressure on Everton from the off, with a couple of corners from the Declan Rice side, but another – delivered by Martin Odegaard – drew dividends. Gabriel flicked the ball on, Pickford got a hand to it, it dropped into a dangerous area at the near post and before a defender could get it away, Ezri Konsa was there to poke home from close range to make it 1-0. I quite enjoyed his post-match interview where he spoke about having to wait a long time for his first Arsenal goal, he only joined in the summer and he’s a defender, but I guess you can’t argue against his desire to get off the mark.

After that, Everton enjoyed a little period of the game where they had some possession, but posed little threat, before Arsenal upped the ante and probably should have gone in at half-time further ahead. A lovely move ended with Eze playing a ball into an area where I thought Gyokeres should have attacked it but he was on his heels a bit and it rolled not far wide – maybe Eze could have taken the shot on himself. Rice then fed Noni Madueke who turned well but dragged his shot wide of the far post with his right foot; Merino had an effort blocked; Madueke nearly produced a superb strike with a brilliant touch, turn, and shot from the edge of the box which fizzed just wide of the near post with Pickford rooted to the spot; Odegaard danced through the defence to see a shot deflected wide; and just before half-time Merino flicked a Rice free kick over the bar.

The only thing Everton had to offer was a chance for Thierno Barry when Ben White was unaware of his presence when trying to head back to his goalkeeper, but David Raya was there to make the save. It was pretty much one way traffic, and we absolutely deserved the lead at the break.

In the second half, there was a scare for Gabriel when he landed badly on his knee making a clearance. When he stayed down I thought ‘Oh crap he’s done his hamstring and his ACL and maybe his entire spine and nervous system’. Arsenal seemed to be readying Cristhian Mosquera to come on and replace him, but the Brazilian got some treatment, stretched himself out, and got back on. I was unsure about this, we’ve seen it happen more than once when a player who is hurt compounds the matter by not coming off immediately, but in this case it worked out well because he was the man to double the lead.

The manager had made a triple sub at that point with Kai Havertz, Bruno Guimaraes and Riccardo Calafiori replacing Gyokeres, Merino and Lewis-Skelly (who had been booked), and it was a nice pass from the summer signing to find Ben White’s overlapping run. He stood up a nice cross to the back post and Gabriel was there to head home for 2-0. I was not at all worried about offside despite a VAR check, White timed his run perfectly, you could see that in real-time, and the replays showed that.

Everton did have a decent chance when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall flashed a header just wide, but really that was about it. There were late cameos for Max Dowman and Martin Zubimendi who took a pointy elbow to the nose and needed treatment for that. Hopefully it doesn’t exclude him from the midweek EFL Cup game, because we need him to be there to start to give Rice a rest.

And that was that. Solid, effective, and with plenty to like about aspects of our performance. Sometimes I feel this Arsenal team can be a bit shot-shy, often looking for the perfect opening before letting fly, and it felt to me like they were instructed to just have a go a bit more yesterday. Merino and Odegaard took five shots each, none of them especially dangerous but it was interesting to note the positions. Four of Odegaard’s were from outside the box, with two of Merino’s from distance (and one from just on the edge). Maybe it’s nothing, just an anomaly, but mixing it up against a team that sat pretty deep is a good idea in my opinion.

We’re very happy with the victory, the performance and the week, because we were given a terrible schedule. Playing Sunday afternoon, then Wednesday night in Munich, coming here really late on Thursday and then having to play again in the Premier League against a really tough opponent on Saturday at 3pm. We have overcome some injuries, and I’m really proud of the mentality of the team in the conditions today.

And paid tribute to his central defensive goalscorers, in particular Konsa who has had a strong start to his Arsenal career:

The two centre-backs scored the goals today. We want to be the best in every phase of play, and we won’t stop until we do it. [Konsa is] unbelievable. To come to a club like Arsenal with no pre-season, Saliba is here and other players, and to position yourself in that manner with the naturality he has and put in the performances he has – the chemistry with Gabi that is so solid – is so difficult to do. We’re lucky to have him.

So a clean sheet, a first half goal, a set-piece goal at long last too, and three points, it’s hard to argue. You can see where we could improve, more efficiency in the final third is going to be an ongoing conversation this season I feel, but I think the manager is right to be proud of his team after a Sunday > Wednesday > Saturday schedule provided a real test – in trying conditions too – and his team came through it very, very well.

There’s a midweek game against Fleetwood to think about next, before what is always a difficult trip to Anfield next weekend. But after that defeat to Brighton, the team has generated some momentum, and let’s hope we can keep that going.

Before I go today, a word of thanks to Andrew and Lewis for keeping things going in my absence, and my apologies that we didn’t have a post-Bayern Arsecast for you. I’d been feeling a bit unwell for a few days, went to A&E to get checked out, and after doing that they decided to keep me in hospital for a bit. Having run a whole loads of tests, and with a need to then wait for results, they let me home on Friday evening. So it’s not a clean bill of health, but they’d done as much as they can at that point.

I just want to say thanks to everyone who was in touch and sent messages/emails – it’s much appreciated. It’s not that you take your health for granted, but when something happens out of the blue it does make you appreciate how life was the day before you found out something wasn’t quite right. I don’t think there’s anything more scary than starting at a white wall in a hospital before they feed you head first into a machine that makes Berlin techno-noises. There’s just too much time to be left alone with your own thoughts, and I don’t like it!

Anyway, we’ll wait and see, and for now things continue as normal. We’ll have an Arsecast Extra for you tomorrow as usual, and in the meantime look after yourselves. Have a great Sunday folks.

#1720. Real Madrid transfer news: Los Blancos make key decision ahead of January window

By Axel Clody | 02 Nov 2026 11:11

Two months before the opening of the winter transfer window, Real Madrid have already made an important decision about it.

Real Madrid had a very turbulent last transfer window. Following the arrival of Jose Mourinho, the Spanish giants renewed part of their squad and invested more than £190m, notably on Yan Diomande and Marc Cucurella. They also parted with squad players such as Fran Garcia and Gonzalo Garcia, recovering £50m.

The next winter transfer window should be much less intense in the Madrid offices.

According to AS, Real Madrid will not be concerned with the next transfer window. The current third-placed side in La Liga do not feel the need to strengthen their squad in the middle of the season.

The club hierarchy believe this group can end a trophy drought of a year and a half. The few injuries recorded at the start of the season and possible winter opportunities are not enough to consider signing anyone this winter.

In recent days, there have been rumours about possible returns of Jacobo Ramon and Nico Paz, who are shining at Como.

‘Real Madrid’s executives have not yet made any decision on the futures of the players on whom they hold a buy-back option, and nothing is expected to be decided before next spring,’ the Spanish outlet says.

The need for a reinforcement in midfield this winter has also been mentioned in the press, but that is not the case internally.

However, Real Madrid could open the door to departures in the next transfer window. That will only happen if a player asks to leave and Mourinho does not oppose it. AS says, however, that this ‘does not seem very likely for now’.

#1719. Everyone loves a good comedy

The Premier League continues to amuse this season, with Man Utd’s troubles continuing after a 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth at Old Trafford yesterday. It probably spells the end of Michael Carrick as manager, which is a bit of a shame. I loved his work. Up there with Ruben Amorim and Ruud van Nistelrooy for me. Legend, in my opinion.

Obviously though, United’s problems run deeper than the man on the touchline. The dressing room is a toxic mess, which is quite funny because that’s the kind of thing Sir Jimmy Ratcliffe is an expert in given his position at INEOS – one of the UK’s great polluters. Still, whatever happens at Man Utd, however he continues to ruin internal morale by installing soup kitchens and firing staff like they’re not people worth a moment’s consideration, I guess he can just enjoy life as bigoted old tax-exile in Monaco, wondering why it is that he feels ‘his’ country isn’t what it used to be as he avoids contributing to society by paying his fair share.

I saw a story the other the day in the Athletic about how 72 year old Ratcliffe once went to the physio room to offer players advice on stretching because he’d run the London Marathon. If that doesn’t tell you exactly how dysfunctional that club is, nothing will. Except, of course, for the results on the pitch, the way they play, their position in the table, and the fact that senior players are basically saying ‘F*ck this! I have to go public’ in post-match interviews. But honestly, imagine Stan Kroenke at London Colney giving Viktor Gyokeres advice on how to hold it up, because he’d spent years holding up objections to one of his massively obscene land deals.

I can’t say I have a lot of time for either Lisandro Martinez or Bruno Fernandes, and they will probably become targets for being outspoken. Maybe they were wrong to do it, maybe as captain Fernandes is entirely the wrong kind of character when your club is in this kind of a situation, but it still speaks to the mess that exists on and off the pitch that they’ve said what they’ve said. Yes, it’s very, very entertaining for all of us, but in a purely objective sense, it says a lot.

I remember when Ralf Rangnick was boss there for a while, and he was roundly pilloried because results weren’t good, but he was spot on four or five years ago when he spoke about how the place needed an entire rebuild. I think he said something like it required open heart surgery, and he was absolutely right. All this time later, that operation is still required, but they have a xenophobic egomaniac in charge who would happily deport most of his playing staff if they weren’t talented footballers, and who continues to oversee bad decision after bad decision. Most of the club is still owned by the Glazers who never gave a shit anyway, and as Arsenal fans we know this kind of ownership structure is no good. Now they’ll probably just repeat the cycle where some ex-player will come in on an interim basis, get a few half decent results, and that wobbly-mouthed halfwit Rio Ferdinand will do a giddy dance on live TV about giving him a six year contract because he ‘knows the club’. Which is probably what they’ll do.

Welcome to the hot-seat Darren Fletcher/John O’Shea/Phil Jones/Henning Berg/David May/Alan Smith (the evil blue-lipped one)/Nani. Oh, please, give it to Phil Neville. Listening to Gary tie himself in knots every week on Sky would be amazing. Surely a reward for all us having to listen to him for all these years. Come on universe, you owe us this at least.

I saw a clip of a renowned Man Utd streamer going mad during their humiliating defeat at home yesterday, scornfully saying ‘But it’s Bournemouth! It’s Bournemouth!’, which tells you plenty. Anyone who has watched Bournemouth over the last few seasons would understand that even with a new manager in charge, they are a really good side with good players who can hurt you. The arrogance, the hubris, to think that just because their ground only holds a fraction of the capacity of Ancient Trafford, you are entitled to win the game.

I’m not saying he is part of the problem, per se, but if that level of delusion exists within their fanbase despite all the evidence they’ve had presented to them – right in front of their very eyes! – then it probably tells you something about the job that club needs to do. Thankfully for all of us, they appear to have a collection of people in charge thoroughly incapable of doing that. Sir Jimmy might brilliant at pumping petrochemical run-off into the atmosphere and poisoning wildlife, but he seems to be something of a footballing idiot. And quite hilariously, their current chief executive is a man called Omar Berrada, who used to work at Man City where two of his job titles between 2011 and 2015 were ‘Head of International Business Development’ and ‘Director of Partnership Sales’. What an interesting timeline that is, eh?!

I know we all have our issues with Arsenal, and we’ve been through some stuff over the years, but on this Monday morning as we begin a new week, let’s take a moment to be thankful for where we are right now. One decision can absolutely change the trajectory of your football club, and for us that was the appointment of Mikel Arteta. Reading lately that other options were considered ahead of him gave me a shudder, because we absolutely would not be in the same rude health if we’d gone down those particularly avenues.

Which is to say, the very best of luck to the Steve Bruce – Gary Pallister dream team.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now, but we will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on today. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around noon or so. Until then, have a good one.

#1716. A chance for rotation and rest as we face Fleetwood Town

We’re in EFL Cup action this evening, taking on Fleetwood Town at Highbury Stadium (not that one). Tonight’s opposition sit 18th in League Two, and this will surely influence Mikel Arteta’s team selection. There are players I just do not want to see this evening. Not just from the start, but not in the squad at all.

The likes of Declan Rice, Gabriel, Ezri Konsa, Martin Odegaard have all played a lot and could use a night off, and I would also include the two wide players we have fit – Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze. With injuries to Bukayo Saka and Christos Tzolis, we’re very light in that area of the pitch, and we do not need to risk them in a game like this. There’s still plenty of scope for rotation, and there are some senior players who could use some minutes, as well as an opportunity to fill out the bench with Academy lads.

You imagine we’ll see starts for Kepa, Martin Zubimendi (assuming his nose isn’t too sore after the weekend), Cristhian Mosquera, Piero Hincapie, Mikel Merino, maybe Jurrien Timber, Myles Lewis-Skelly, and possibly Bruno Guimaraes, but also it’s an opportunity for Marli Salmon and Max Dowman again, both of whom started in the last round against Ipswich. Dowman played centrally that evening, in the Odegaard role, and got two goals, but I wonder if tonight he might be used out wide as we rest Madueke.

After that, young players like Ife Ibrahim and Theo Julienne will be hoping for minutes to add to the ones they picked up in the last round, while forwards like Ceadach O’Neill and Igor Tyjon might fancy their chances of being included. This is a kind draw ahead of a weekend trip to Anfield, and with Liverpool playing Chelsea tomorrow night, it’s an opportunity for the manager to ease the burden on the guys who have played a lot as well as giving the next generation a chance too.

I think we’ll also see Viktor Gyokeres up front, and the Swedish international could really do with a goal. He’s on a barren streak (in club terms at least), that stretches back to May 2nd, and it’s now 15 games without a goal. Even though his minutes have been a bit scant this season, that’s a record that’s hanging over him and one he’ll want to put right. A goal, or goals, against a League Two side in this competition will always have that little caveat applied, but it ought to be a real opportunity for him to build a little goalscoring confidence, so fingers crossed he can do exactly that.

Speaking about tonight’s game, Arteta said:

Every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve to do that, and then try to win and try to play better than them.

So, let’s see how it plays out later on, kick off is 20.00 in this part of the world.

Elsewhere, while I find the concept of individual awards in football completely counter-intuitive to what makes the game as compelling as it is, I did want to mention Bukayo Saka winning the Socrates Award at the Ballon d’Or ceremony last night. The official website reports that: “Bukayo and his family have worked with multiple charities, including long-term projects with Big Shoe, providing medical care and humanitarian aid for children and families in need in London and around the world.”

And yet, they are often held up as an example of people who earn too much for doing too little. I remember during Covid, politicians singled out football players as those who should set an example by taking wage cuts or making charity donations or supporting the health services, while ignoring those who – less publicly – earn far, far more. But as we can see here, someone like Bukayo Saka (and he’s far from alone too), uses what his talent has provided to help others, and while I’m sure he doesn’t do it for awards or recognition, this spotlight on what he does can help the causes he supports.

This is an individual award worth highlighting, and you can see the ceremony and his speech about it below.

#1713. Bruno Fernandes has 'TARNISHED' his Man United legacy after his public criticism of Michael Carrick - and peace talks might be 'papering over the cracks', warns Alan Shearer

Published: 15:30 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 15:47 EDT, 30 October 2026

Alan Shearer has claimed that Bruno Fernandes has 'tarnished' his Manchester United legacy following his fallout with Michael Carrick over the last couple of weeks.

The Red Devils captain raised eyebrows when he questioned his manager's tactics after their side's 4-1 defeat by Como in the Champions League, and was subsequently left out of the team for their later loss against Bournemouth.

He spoke out just a matter of days after Lisandro Martinez had questioned United's activity behind the scenes, and left his United future in doubt.

That's according to all-time Premier League leading scorer Shearer, who claimed Fernandes' previous success is now marred.

'Fernandes is going to have to go out and perform, which he hasn't done for large parts this season,' Shearer told Betfair. 'I know he's been Man United’s go-to player for a long time now, he's been their best player, but it's no way for the captain to behave.

'He owes the manager a performance, he owes the club a performance, and he owes the fans a performance.'

Bruno Fernandes (right) has 'tarnished' his Manchester United legacy after criticising Michael Carrick (left), according to Alan Shearer

He added: 'I think he has tarnished his legacy at the club. I think the reaction that you saw at the end of the game against Bournemouth last week was pretty telling whose side the fans are on and it's Michael Carrick's, not Bruno Fernandes’, despite what he's done for the club.

'Whether that was part of him speaking to the manager and thinking, woah, I have got this wrong here. I don't know.'

Fernandes and Carrick held clear-the-air talks after the 3-0 Bournemouth loss, and many expect the midfielder to return to the side this weekend against Chelsea.

But it's unclear what will follow. Shearer, meanwhile, isn't convinced all is well.

'Fernandes and Carrick’s peace talks could’ve and probably should’ve happened before the game last week,' he added. 'Then there might not have been as much noise.

'Are they just papering over the cracks? I've been in a situation myself where I've not really got on with the manager in terms of Ruud Gullit and I guess you'd have to be on the inside to know what's really going on, but it would seem strange for him saying what he said, being left out and then being reinstated and then walking out as captain this week.

'It's not a good look, is it? It's pretty chaotic.'

Shearer suggested that crisis talks between Carrick and Fernandes may be 'papering over the cracks' amid the side's struggles

Old Trafford bosses decided not to sack Carrick with United in 16th place in the Premier League table, one point clear of the relegation zone.

The 45-year-old still faces a battle to improve results and performances and convince his employers that he remains the right person for the job.

Sources confirmed that Carrick has been given a second chance, and said that everyone is focused on showing a response on the pitch at Stamford Bridge following United’s worst start to a league season in 40 years.

The United boss was left in limbo after chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox held crisis talks on Monday with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

The first indications that Carrick had earned a reprieve came shortly before 8am on Tuesday when he arrived at Carrington dressed in a club tracksuit and oversaw training as the players returned after a day off.

He had also turned up at the training ground on Monday but was there to watch United’s Under-21s play in a behind-closed-doors game against Hull City alongside his No2 Steve Holland and Under-18s coach Darren Fletcher. He stayed for three hours before leaving with his son Jacey, a member of United’s Under-18s.

#1711. Martin Odegaard bails out comically wasteful Arsenal

For much of this sticky night in Naples, Arsenal appeared to be starting the new Champions League campaign the same way they finished the last one: by erroneously smashing the ball into the stands behind the goal.

Memories of Gabriel Magalhães’s ballooned penalty in the final against Paris St-Germain remain fresh in the mind, and here his team-mates were lining up to produce their own versions. Bukayo Saka and Piero Hincapié, especially, delivered astonishing misses which were closer to entering orbit than the opposition net.

Thankfully for Arsenal, though, there was one player who was in no mood to relive the frustration of that shoot-out loss 14 weeks ago. Martin Odegaard has started this season in truly fabulous form and here he scored a truly fabulous late goal, fizzed into the corner from range, to cap another inventive individual performance and earn three points for his team.

Great play 😮‍💨Martin Ødegaard rounds off a wonderful passing move for Arsenal 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FrH6gW8Ak4

In five matches this season, Odegaard has already scored four goals. That is three more than he managed in the whole of last season. The Arsenal captain is fit again and he is flowing. As ever, when Odegaard flows, Arsenal flow.

“That’s what we need, the players with that mindset to decide the game and play with that personality,” said Mikel Arteta. “He has got that edge. He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games.”

In the end it was a thoroughly deserved victory for the Premier League side, who were superior to Napoli in every department. Were it not for their comically bad finishing, they would have guaranteed the result long before Odegaard’s 75th-minute strike.

Their expected goals figure suggested they should have scored more than four goals, compared to Napoli’s 0.22. In total, they registered 26 shots – the most of any Arsenal team on record in a single Champions League match, and the most on record a Napoli team has ever faced.

“With the amount of chances we generated, the scoreline has to reflect a very different result,” said Arteta. “The number of players that got into this situation, the amount of situations that we generated in various ways was something that pleased me a lot.”

There was, almost inevitably, another clean sheet for Arteta’s side. They had the best defence in the Champions League last season, conceding only seven goals in 15 matches, and they were largely untroubled here. Ezri Konsa was once again excellent, in only his second start for the club. He successfully wrapped up Rasmus Hojlund, the former Manchester United centre-forward, and was as calm in possession as the absent William Saliba would have been. A potential injury to right-back Ben White was a concern, though.

The Champions League is the one that Arsenal have never won and, you suspect, the one that Arteta really wants. Success in this competition would elevate Arsenal to a higher level as a club and fully establish Arteta as one of the great coaching minds of his generation.

To lose last season’s final in such painful circumstances clearly hurt the Arsenal manager, who was visibly distraught after that shoot-out defeat despite the obvious delight of winning the Premier League title. If you could give him the choice between retaining the league this season or leading Arsenal to their first European Cup, he would surely pick the latter.

Arsenal have now won THIRTEEN UCL League Phase games in a row 🔴🔥 pic.twitter.com/UmcfMYO13r

A trip to Naples in the first round of the league phase made for a lovely opening tie: atmospheric, intense and competitive. Napoli have had a difficult start to their campaign, losing two of three Serie A games so far, but they possess real quality and have a top manager in Massimiliano Allegri.

Even at the age of 35, the great Kevin De Bruyne still has power in his boots and schemes in his mind. When he tested Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya from range in the first half, it would have triggered horrible flashbacks in the minds of the travelling supporters. In his previous 17 starts against Arsenal for Manchester City, De Bruyne had scored eight goals and registered four assists. Thankfully for Arsenal, it was the only moment in which De Bruyne really threatened.

Throughout this game, Arsenal moved the ball around with precision and purpose. They created an extraordinary amount of chances, with Saka and Hincapié missing the best of them. Saka’s effort in the first half, when one-v-one with the goalkeeper, was strangely erratic. Hincapié’s opportunity, meanwhile, was laughable. Two yards out from goal, he somehow put the ball onto the running track that surrounds the pitch at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

Despite all the wasted chances, Arsenal kept going. Odegaard, in particular, kept probing. His goal was gorgeous: a swift exchange of passes between him, White and Christos Tzolis resulted in the Arsenal captain firing his effort from the edge of the area. Delicate build-up, ferocious finish.

In keeping with the theme of the night, Arsenal should have scored more. Noni Madueke, for example, missed a one-v-one when it seemed like he had all the time in the world. But Odegaard’s intervention eventually proved to be enough, as he once again stood forward as Arsenal’s match-winner.

That’s all from us, but we’ll be back tomorrow night to bring you Man Utd’s return to the Champions League against Sabah!

"I think the chemistry, especially in the front players, has been exceptional." ✨Mikel Arteta tells @AnitaNnekaJones how impressed he's been by the connection between Martin Ødegaard and Christos Tzolis 🤝 pic.twitter.com/J6VOAMk4Lm

Arsenal extend their #UCL unbeaten streak 👏 pic.twitter.com/wFBga6lNrN

"We missed so many big chances"Mikel Arteta shares his thoughts after Arsenal's victory over Napoli 💭🎙️ @DannyJamieson | 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/zT2bHcPoiH

Before all of that, Arsenal will now have to turn their attention to the Stadium of Light as they travel to Sunderland on Saturday.

They then face Ipswich Town in the EFL Cup on Tuesday night, before travelling to Brighton on the weekend.

Tue, November 24: Borussia Dortmund (H) 8pm

“Everything runs through Martin Odegaard,” said Cole on TNT Sports. “He can stand still and find space. He is at the peak of his powers and it is beautiful to watch.

“You can’t help but love watching him play his football.”

Plenty of praise for Martin Odegaard on TNT, with former Arsenal man Martin Keown heralding the captain’s behaviour.

“He’s setting an example to his players. He’s fitter, he’s hungry, and he did his talking on the pitch. He came good for his team.”

Couple that with his impressive chemistry with new arrival Christos Tzolis, and there is a lot of goal-scoring potential there this season. Three of the winger’s four assists have been for his captain, and we’re barely a month into the season.

The action has concluded around Europe tonight so here are your final scores from this week’s second night of European football:

Napoli did not register a shot on target in that second half, and it is clear how much Arsenal just dominated to keep the pressure on.

It could easily have been three or four goals for Arsenal had they had better finishing, but either way, they did not let their heads go down.

They kept pushing to see out the result and got the job done. Arteta will be very happy with that away result.

This has not been Arsenal’s most clinical performance but they got the job done.

Here is the goal that won it for them, courtesy of their captain:

Great play 😮‍💨Martin Ødegaard rounds off a wonderful passing move for Arsenal 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FrH6gW8Ak4

Napoli are fighting, but Arsenal hold fast.

Milinković-Savić waves his players downfield for the final minute but Olivera can’t control the ball well.

Four minutes will be added on here as Napoli are being urged on by their fans.

Arsenal need to hold onto the ball and manage the game intelligently here. Zubimendi goes in for a challenge though and hauls down his man, and Napoli get the ball back. Odegaard goes into the book for his protests.

Napoli again, still trying to get their goal and De Bruyne gives them a chance with a through ball to David Neres, but the striker can’t get on the ball.

Arsenal are almost caught as the ball falls to De Bruyne on the left of the box, with a clear look at Raya in goal, but the Belgian crosses the ball thinking he’s got a team-mate there to put it away but there is no one and it is a huge let-off for Arsenal.

Napoli with every man forward lose the ball and suddenly Zubimendi finds himself on the break. With Madueke on his right, he feeds the winger who gets into space in the box to be one-on-one with Milinković-Savić. But the Arsenal man hesitates and the keeper spreads himself, blocking Madueke’s eventual shot. He can’t turn around to get on the rebound and cuts is back for Tzolis, whose own shot is then blocked.

With just a few minutes to go, Arsenal make their final change.

Ben White appeared to be in a little bit of discomfort a few minutes ago. He’s now been replaced by Martin Zubimendi for the final 10 minutes of this game. Declan Rice appears to have moved to right-back.

Martin Odegaard has played some outstanding football tonight (again) and that is an absolutely outstanding goal. The delicacy of the build-up and then the ferocity of the finish. Four goals in five games for Odegaard this season.

There will be alarm bells ringing for Allegri and Napoli, as they are heading for their third defeat on the trot. They have not created much of anything in this second half and you have to imagine that Arsenal will now make life very difficult for them.

To be exact, they have had a grand total of one shot in the second half.

Napoli will have to push now, and make more changes, bringing on Lorenzo Lucca and David Neres for Rasmus Hojlund and Stanislav Lobotka.

The breakthrough comes and of course it is Odegaard! Finally they get their moment, hacing recycled the ball on the edge of the area.

Rice just passes it out to him off a nice ball from Tzolis and the captain rifles a low shot into the far bottom corner.

Rice loses the ball in midfield and fouls Olivera as he tries to recover it.

Before they take the free kick though, Arsenal make more changes. Kai Havertz and Noni Madueke come on for Gyokeres and Saka.

Guimaraes to Saka before the winger sends the ball back to Odegaard on the edge of the box. He lifts a ball into the centre of the box where there are a lot of bodies, but Tzolis snatches at it and sends the ball into the rafters.

Sums up the game so far really for Arsenal.

There is definitely a goal in here somewhere. Napoli are still waiting and searching for their goal, and Arsenal will keep throwing shots at the wall until something sticks.

There are the subs, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze are the ones to make way.

Christos Tzolis and Bruno Guimaraes getting ready to come on.

At the same time, Favasuli makes a neat little run on the right trying to get to the touchline and pull the ball back, but Raya is able to pick it up easily.

That was almost it for Napoli, Hojlund with a great run in behind. He gets into the box one-on-one against his defender as Raya retreats. The challenge is perfectly timed though as he tries to get his shot off and the ball goes spinning off to the side.

Neither side are looking clinical in front of goal though as Arsenal take the ball down the other end, and Declan Rice can only send another shot over the bar.

Saka tries to take another chance on the edge of the box, but he loses the ball.

Napoli try to seize their moment on the break, with Favasuli releasing down the left side. He looks for Hojlund in the middle of the field, but his cross is just not good enough and Raya comes out to collect the high ball.

Politano and Alisson Santos make way for Antonio Vergara and Constantino Favasuli.

Though the hosts came out on the front foot, it has been all Arsenal since then, so Allegri will be hoping these changes can shift the momentum.

Alisson Santos gets past White on the sideline, and makes the run down the left. He tries to find De Bruyne making the run in the middle but it is intercepted and Arsenal take the ball back up the field.

Napoli are getting ready to make some changes.

Arsenal probing again, with Rice, Saka, Odegaard and White exchanging passes on the right edge of the box. Saka tries a low ball in but it’s blocked before it gets to Gyokeres.

Napoli are sitting so deep, you have to assume they are just waiting for an opportunity to counter. Even so, Arsenal are doing well to keep the ball moving around and try and find space. The hosts are really trying not to concede first.

Another wasted chance for Arsenal! Great play from Odegaard lifting a little ball into the centre of the box, which is flicked on towards goal. It falls to Hincapié in the six-yard box but as he tries to poke it into the goal, the Ecuadorian sends it flying over the bar.

Napoli have every man behind the ball right now as Arsenal get some possession.

Arsenal’s turn now, as White gets himself into a good position on the right side of the box, exchanging passes with Odegaard and Saka.

Saka tries to send a ball into the box, but it’s blocked and sent out the sideline as Napoli remain disciplined and shut down the space.

That momentum falls apart for Napoli as Oliveira fouls Gyokeres as the strikers comes in to defend.

Napoli are starting with some pressure here..

Napoli have changed their keepers at half-time. Meret received some treatment in the first half and has been taken off, replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic. It’s his first appearance of the season.

Arsenal with the better of the first half, but unable to find the breakthrough.

Liverpool have equalised at Anfield after Marcos Llorente put Atlético Madrid ahead. Dominik Szoboszlai is the man to put the ball in the back of the net – to the great relief of Andoni Iraola I’m sure.

Reigning champions PSG are 3-0 up against Slovan, with a quick double coming from Mr Ballon D’or himself, Ousmane Dembélé. Ferran Torres scored the third.

Sporting vs Galatasaray also level at 1-1 so it’s really all to play for in the next 45 minutes. Stay tuned!

That’s the final action of the half, and nothing separates the two sides at the break. Both with three shots on target, though Arsenal have taken 13 shots to Napoli’s four.

Both teams could have stolen a goal to take the lead, but they will have to wait for the second period for the opportunity.

Arsenal get a corner which is delivered really well to the far post, but as it’s headed in, there is no space for White to turn and shoot from the six-yard box. He tries to lay it off for Hincapié but Meret gets low to grab it.

Arsenal have created more than enough chances to be three or four goals clear here. That miss by Saka was the best one yet, and the England winger will be in disbelief at the spooned nature of his finish. It looked a certain goal. Shocker.

Arsenal get another great chance as Odegaard sends a perfect ball to Saka as he makes the run into the box on the right side. The winger stays onside but Lobotka does enough to put him off and Saka sends it over the bar.

Napoli are first into the book as Gilmour fouls Eze 35 yards out.

Arsenal take the free kick but end up passing the ball around the edge of the box. Eventually Odegaard lifts a high ball into the box, but Meret punches it away confidently.

Konsa does really well to hold up Alisson Santos as he makes a very speedy run down the left, keeping him from sending a ball into the box.

The game is opening up now, as Saka makes a run of his own down the right, with Gyokeres in the box but Napoli keep tight and Rrahmani does well to stop the ball reaching the striker.

A good save from Raya as Hojlund again feeds the wings from the centre of the field. Politano makes a great run in from the right side with the ball and takes a curling shot with his left foot on the edge of the box.

Arsenal’s keeper collects and then minutes later his side have a shot of their own, but Saka can only send it over the bar.

Saka again gets enough time on the right edge of the box to send a low ball to Rice in the right corner. His shot goes over the bar and we’re having an impromptu drinks break as Meret gets some treatment.

Treat yourself to a hydration break of your own.

Napoli coming close as Hojlund fed in the centre, one-on-one with Konsa, trying to turn at the top of the box. He dinks the ball into the path of the running De Bruyne, whose shot is blocked by Konsa, who scrambles back quickly.

Hincapié sends a cross in from the left which almost catches Meret out at the near post as the keeper scrambles across to push it away.

Now it’s Napoli’s turn as Lobotka sends a long ball down the left to Alisson Santos, who sends a great cross in to the box. Konsa just does enough to put him off and it meets Rice in the centre of the box, for the midfielder to clear.

Saka comes in again on his left foot, with a series of short passes between Odegaard and Rice, but his shot is blocked as two defenders shut him down.

Another attempt for Arsenal as Odegaard gets forward and passes to Eze on the left wing. He drives in and takes a shot with his right foot from just inside the box, but he drags it wide of the target.

Good start to this game. Plenty going on. Arsenal look dangerous and capable of pinning Napoli deep into their own half, but the Italians have threatened on the break. De Bruyne’s shot from range would have triggered some nasty flashbacks for the Arsenal fans but, thankfully for them, it was straight at Raya.

Great chance from Arsenal as Eze pulls away at the back post and connects with the ball to send a header into the box. Merino connects with a diving header of his own but it’s straight at Meret and tipped over the bar.

Arsenal again biding their time until Rice plays a neat ball to White on the right edge of the boxm which he lifts into the box. No one around to do anything with it and Meret collects.

Arsenal being patient on the edge of the box moving the ball around, but eventually it breaks down with Eze losing the ball and then fouling De Bruyne as he tries to break away.

The Napoli players feel that should have been a card.

Di Lorenzo again looks to find space down the centre of the field but sends the ball out to Politano again on the right wing, who lofts a very high ball towards the back post but Raya collects with confidence.

Di Lorenzo makes a great run onto a long ball on the left side, racing down the sideline. He sends a ball across to find De Bruyne in the centre of the field, and the midfielder takes a great shot, which Raya can’t hold on to. White reacts to clear but Napoli are having a good spell.

Politano is the next to force a save from the Arsenal keeper with a shot from the right corner of the box, keeping their visitors very much on their toes.

Arsenal dominating possession in the early stages, just testing the Napoli defence. The stadium is quite quiet and we can hear the travelling fans declaring their love for their team.

Free kick for the visitors as Eze is fouled 40 yards out. Odegaard takes and sends a high ball into the centre of the box, which Gabriel can’t quite control.

Arsenal come again as Gyokeres sends a cross into the box from the left and Saka tries an overhead kick but it is straight into the centre of the goal and Meret has little trouble.

Rice again but the keeper comes to collect and sets the counter free.

Hojlund makes a great run and feeds Alisson Santos on the left side. He tries to cut in but is well marked by White and he can only send his shot over the bar from inside the box.

Arsenal get their first corner as Eze finds himself in a central position at the top of the box, and plays neat one-two with Gyokeres, but his shot takes a big deflection.

Rice goes to the corner flag, and sends in a good ball, headed out by Napoli for another corner.

Arsenal probing on the right wing, with White, Odegaard and Saka overlapping nicely. The captain feeds White and he passes in a neat little ball to Saka just inside the box. He tries a shot, but it’s blocked.

Napoli are getting back very quickly when Arsenal are pressing.

Marín sends a nice high ball across the field to find Politano on the right side. He feeds De Bruyne on the edge of the box and the Belgian tries a shot at Raya, curling it with his right foot, but with not much on it, Raya collects in the middle of goal.

Both teams getting little spells on the ball to get going.

Arsenal are keeping tight as Napoli try and play the ball out from the back and the long ball out to Hojlund is easily collected for Raya.

You can hear the Arsenal fans in loud voice, accompanied by plenty of jeers and whistles from the home fans.

The players are lining up around the centre circle, with a minute of silence for the victims of the tragedy in Nepal.

#1709. Fleetwood Town 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 pens): A dismal night at Highbury

Arsenal crashed out of the Carabao Cup last night, going down 5-3 on penalties to Fleetwood Town after a 1-1 draw in normal time.

Mikel Arteta made changes, as you’d expect, with starts for young players Marli Salmon, Max Dowman and Ceadach O’Neill, while thus far peripheral senior men like Martin Zubimendi, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie also came in for what ought to have been valuable playing time. He also decided, somewhat curiously in my opinion, to start both of his strikers, with Viktor Gyokeres up front and Kai Havertz behind him in midfield.

There was a surreal start to the game when the referee spotted a drone hovering above Highbury Stadium and stopped play. I’m unsure what the big issue was however. Was he worried about player safety, TV rights? Whatever it was, we were stalled for 8 minutes until it was sorted out, not ideal for both sets of players on a night when conditions weren’t exactly clement.

When play began again Arsenal dominated the ball but struggled to test the home side. Hincapie headed a Dowman cross over, before the 16 year old had a clear sight of goal but scuffed his right-footed shot wide. In the middle, Gyokeres looked unhappy as if the ball should have been squared but the shot was the right decision, the execution of it was the issue.

Then, Fleetwood scored. We weren’t competitive enough around the second ball after a long kick from the goalkeeper, they played it forward, and Aaron Loupalo-Bi got the wrong side of Salmon before firing home through the legs of Illan Meslier. It’s not great defending from the 17 year old, but it’s one of those moments as a young player that are inevitable and that ultimately you learn from. He was superb against Ipswich in the last round, and given how badly we fared further forward with more experienced players, I don’t think we should give this much more than a passing mention.

Decent balls in from Dowman gave Havertz and Timber headed chances which they spurned before the break, and that was the extent of our attacking play in that first period. So, it was no surprise when the manager made changes at the break with Ben White and Martin Odegaard replacing Salmon and Timber. It meant a bit of a reshuffle, and early in the second half we found an equaliser.

O’Neill, who looked lively on the left, played a decent ball in from that side, Fleetwood’s defenders didn’t deal with it, Gyokeres – as he does too often – fell over, but on his way down touched it beyond the keeper for 1-1. And that should have been the point at which the game changed in our favour, but what we produced subsequent to the goal was just dismal. Odegaard made us a little bit better, but around him few others stepped up.

Havertz was abysmal missing a great chance after Odegaard’s clever pass put him through, and Gyokeres completing 5 of 9 passes all night against League Two opposition illustrates the limitations of his game in stark fashion. When we need a focal point up front, he just cannot provide it. Eberechi Eze came on and made little difference, and while perhaps there’s some mitigation for Martin Zubimendi playing with a broken nose, he completely failed to impose himself on the game in any meaningful way for a player of his calibre. And then everything was compounded by the red card.

After a bit of a scramble near the touchline there was a strong tackle on Dowman, one which took ball but also slid through on the man. He took exception to it, there was a very slight retaliatory movement with his leg which sparked a bit of a melee (Ben White was right on the scene to protect his teammate), and the referee adjudged it sufficient to send Dowman off. I think it’s very, very harsh.

I don’t think the challenge from the Fleetwood player is quite as bad as some make out, but I can understand why Max reacted. He shouldn’t have done that, but you can’t send a player off for that. It wasn’t a kick, it wasn’t violent conduct, and I think an experienced referee should have been able to sort that out with a couple of yellow cards. Whether Arsenal will appeal the severity of a three match ban remains to be seen, but I think they have a good case to do so if they choose.

What I really didn’t like, however, was Arteta’s reaction as Dowman went off. He clearly gave him an earful, and said afterwards, “Something that we discussed already before the match.”

A little earlier there had been a confrontation between Odegaard and a Fleetwood player, and I think we can all understand the manager warning his players not to rise to any kind of bait. Nevertheless, Max Dowman is 16, and the manager’s job is to protect him. It doesn’t mean he has to be mollycoddled, it doesn’t mean he shouldn’t face the internal consequences of being shown a red card, but that should have played out in the dressing room, not on the touchline and on live TV. Arteta has done incredible work at this football club, but he’s not infallible, and in my opinion he got this one really wrong – regardless of how frustrated he might be with the reaction from Dowman.

There was a late flurry from Arsenal as we looked to avoid penalties. The keeper made a very good save from Ben White, Odegaard had a shot which required another stop, and just before the end there was a really presentable chance for Havertz from an Eze cross which he headed tamely wide with no conviction. A moment which summed his own performance, and that of the team. Feeble.

So then penalties. Fleetwood made no mistake with five solid spot kicks, we made one through Bruno Guimaraes, and that was that. A massive win for the home side, and fair play to them for it. It’s a night that will live long in the history of that club, and this is what cup football can throw up. It’s not the first time we’ve been the giant killed by a lower league side, but I really don’t think we can have any complaints because of how poorly we played overall. Congrats to them.

First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through the next round. The manner that they have done it, and for us a very sad day. There is nothing to criticise the players for their attitude, their application. The determination – you could see that was there from the start.

The team keeps trying and trying with the ball with chances, shots and especially shots that we had not to score many more goals. Then you don’t capitalise, then you cannot go through to the next round. Unfortunately, we are out.

I will say I think that’s a very generous assessment of our performance. Protective almost, in a way the comments about Dowman were not. There’s a big difference between having a lot of the ball and making that possession count, and while nights like this can happen, upsets are part of football, too many players out there last night let themselves down. Ahead of a big game at Anfield at the weekend, it’s not ideal, because some of them are going to have to play, and if they’re anything like they were last night, we’ll be in trouble. If you already harbour some concerns about our attacking potency, last night will done nothing to assuage them.

I can’t sit here this morning and say I’m devastated at going out of this competition, but this was a night which produced many more questions than answers. If you were generous you’d say we were rusty and the changed nature of the side meant we lacked cohesion. The other assessment might be that we were absolutely terrible on the night, and even if some players are trying to find some rhythm and match sharpness, we ought to have produced a lot better than that embarrassing load of shit. I tend to connect far more with the latter than the former.

Any defeat at Arsenal creates fallout. That’s something we’re going to have to contend with ahead of the weekend, and the lack of a post-game press conference means legitimate questions about the performance, some individuals, and the manager’s reaction to the sending off will have to wait until Friday, so this is gonna linger like an eggy fart in lift for a few days more.

Update: Seems there was some post-game stuff.

Right, I’ll leave it there for morning. Have a good one folks.

#1708. Morocco squad announcement: Ouahbi faces injury headache before AFCON qualifiers

By Axel Clody | 02 Nov 2026 12:04

With his squad for the Niger games approaching, Mohamed Ouahbi is seeing the treatment room fill up with several important players.

A squad is rarely built without surprises. But when bad news hits the defence, midfield and attack almost at the same time, it ends up considerably disrupting the manager’s plans. Mohamed Ouahbi is experiencing that, just days before the double-header against Niger in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Ismael Saibari, Azzedine Ounahi, Ayoub El Kaabi and Chadi Riad are unavailable for a long period, and Soufiane Rahimi is highly doubtful.

Injured in the clash between Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund, the attacking midfielder has a ruptured syndesmotic ligament in his right ankle. Successfully operated on after his injury in the Klassiker, he should stay out for several months and will miss the games against Niger on 13 and 17 November.

His absence frustrates Ouahbi because of his versatility: the manager has used him both as a number 10 and as a centre-forward, notably during the 2026 World Cup. Saibari brought power, off-the-ball runs and an ability to get into the box.

The Panathinaikos midfielder was seriously injured against Asteras Tripolis (5-1) on 18 October. He suffered damage to the tendon of the right biceps femoris, was operated on and will be out for around two and a half to three months.

Ounahi broke lines by carrying the ball, resisted the press and created in tight spaces. His place could go to Amine Harit, in form with Marseille, while Bilal El Khannouss, Neil El Aynaoui and Ayyoub Bouaddi offer other profiles. None of them exactly reproduces his qualities.

Ayoub El Kaabi, who suffered a fractured left tibia with Olympiacos at the beginning of September, is continuing his rehabilitation after his operation. At 33, he brought his positional sense and his efficiency in the box.

Soufiane Rahimi, who was injured in the hamstring against Shabab Al-Ahli on 22 October, also sees his participation compromised.

Hamza Igamane is getting closer to a return after his serious knee injury but lacks match rhythm. Ouahbi can count on Youssef En-Nesyri or promote a youngster such as Yassir Zabiri.

In defence, the Crystal Palace player suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee against Everton on 22 August. At 23, the left-footed defender, comfortable in build-up and capable of defending in a high line, was supposed to become one of the pillars of the new defence. His absence forces Ouahbi to rely on players who are already in place.

Ilias Akhomach, Soufiane El Fawzi and Youssef Belammari are also weakened and being monitored by the medical staff.

Ouahbi has a big enough pool to field a competitive team against Niger, and this double confrontation can give playing time to less-used players. However, quantity does not replace the experience of Saibari, Ounahi, El Kaabi, Rahimi and Riad: this series of injuries is already upending his squad.

#1706. With McGregor now questioning Celtic's approach, isn't it clear something is badly wrong there?

Published: 14:35 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 16:19 EDT, 30 October 2026

Celtic captain Callum McGregor talking about strikers playing as wingers and his team not having the right shape threw up all manner of issues.

One of them is that time is surely up for Kasper Hogh at centre-forward, £11million club-record signing or not.

When manager Martin O’Neill spoke to the media yesterday, he talked about Callum Osmand really being better through the middle than out on the left. A more pertinent point, though, is that it really doesn’t make sense any longer to keep playing Camilo Duran on the right.

There is, after all, a £9m man in reserve in Haissem Hassan who was signed to play out on that flank.

It just looks ever more like Celtic didn’t really think hard enough about what kind of way they wanted to play when they bought all these blokes.

What’s become clear is that it’s better if it doesn’t involve Hogh, now 13 games without a goal, unless there’s some masterplan to start sticking two up front. Even then, you’d be considering your options.

Callum McGregor was frustrated by his side's display in Wednesday's draw with Dundee Utd

There’s an argument O’Neill doesn’t play to the Dane’s strengths and that does hold water. However, Hogh has got to be able to adapt. If he can’t, what does it say about the decision, and whoever was ultimately responsible for it, to sign him in the first place?

What does a clever, senior figure such as McGregor joining Cameron Carter-Vickers in calling out the structure and organisation of the team say too?

Celtic might still be top of the table, but they’re all over the shop from top to bottom.

If Rangers can’t win the league this term, particularly given the fact they cannot possibly keep spending the way they have been without access to significant funds from UEFA competition, you do wonder when they ever will.

Hibs game looks like being D-day for Robinson at Dons

Aberdeen boss Stephen Robinson really started to bear the look of the condemned man in the wake of his side’s home defeat at the hands of Falkirk during the week.

The bullishness from earlier in the campaign had gone. He gave a thoroughly unconvincing answer on BBC when asked what progress, if any, had been made since the summer. He sounded like a bloke who knows he’s not far from the firing squad.

‘Ultimately, you have to get results,’ he said. ‘Otherwise, you know the inevitable.’

Unless it turns into a procession, a loss to Rangers in Saturday’s Premier Sports Cup semi-final is unlikely to seal his fate. The home game against Hibs next weekend, though, is a different kettle of fish entirely.

Time appears to be running out for Aberdeen manager Stephen Robinson to get things right

If the Dons are to be meeting any of their key performance indicators, they need to be better than Hibs. They need to be finishing above them in the top half of the table. And that’s the bare minimum.

What’s more, the Easter Road side are hardly in tip-top shape. Marink Reedijk’s time as head coach has got off to an underwhelming start. Sporting director Malky Mackay is under pressure over poor recruitment. They are there for the taking.

If Robinson can’t get the better of them at home ahead of an international break, a real time for the club to take stock, he’s in bother.

Those in the Red Army willing to make almost any sacrifice to see him nudged out the door should consider one thing, though.

If the management team get dumped, chances are first-team coach Stephen Craigan will be back all over our tellies and radios in his old role as media mouthpiece. And who really wants that?

#1705. Tactics Column: Midfield carousel unlocks evolution

Anyone else quickly want to think about the Premier League again after Tuesday’s League Cup defeat? Good! We have just the thing for you.

Much has been said about Arsenal’s football over the past few weeks, but Saturday’s win over Everton was a clear step forward in terms of playing against a defensive setup and consistently getting into dangerous areas.

With no Bukayo Saka, who has been the team’s biggest goal threat this season, Mikel Merino came into midfield to play behind Viktor Gyokeres, allowing Martin Odegaard to roam deeper. It was Odegaard’s constant roaming in midfield, with Rice advancing ahead of the ball, and link-up play with Myles Lewis-Skelly, tucking into a midfield role from left-back, that helped stretch Everton and create plenty of opportunities.

Those combinations didn’t directly lead to a goal, but they helped Arsenal dominate and threaten throughout the 2-0 win. A PSG-like fluidity in midfield and plenty of vertical passing looks like a real step forward for this Arsenal side and should make the team a lot more exciting to watch.

#1704. A Thousand Myles

This Monday marks six months since Arsenal defeated Fulham 3-0 at Emirates Stadium. The game offered a rare oasis of calm in an otherwise fraught season of nailbiting wins. The Gunners, in the midst of a five game ‘playoff’ for the league title with Manchester City, as well as a Champions League semi-final against Atletico Madrid on the horizon, raced into a three-goal lead by half-time at the Emirates, earning an uproarious reception as the players made for the tunnel at half-time.

The previous weekend had seen Arsenal labour to a nervy 1-0 win over Newcastle and a stodgy 1-1 away draw with Atletico Madrid. Bukayo Saka had been parachuted back into the team after an extended absence; but it was clear that Mikel Arteta was looking for ways to try to ease the ketchup out of the bottle, so to speak.

Martin Zubimendi, who, at that point had played more league minutes than any other outfield Arsenal player, dropped to the bench. Myles Lewis-Skelly started in midfield for the first time in his short Gunners career. Myles was supposed to start an FA Cup tie at home to Wigan in that position before Riccardo Calafiori was injured in the warm-up, meaning Lewis-Skelly reverted to left-back with Bukayo Saka playing in a central role instead.

The BBC Sport match report for the Fulham game said, ‘Boss Arteta has to be given credit for taking what could be perceived as risk by playing left-back Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield for the first time and leaving out Martin Zubimendi, who has played the most minutes of any outfielder in the Gunners squad. The 19-year-old Lewis-Skelly looked assured in the role and, with Calafiori, Saka and Eberechi Eze all in the side, the Arsenal attack flowed better than it has done for many weeks.’

Myles kept his place for the second leg of the Champions League semi-final against Atleti and again for the crunch away win at West Ham. He then started the Champions League semi-final. Probably a week prior to that Fulham game, many Arsenal fans were talking of an inevitable summer sale following the purchases of Piero Hincapie at left-back and Martin Zubimendi in midfield.

His homegrown status made him a potentially attractive sale. His path appeared to be blocked. The talk clearly wasn’t lost on Lewis-Skelly. When he posted a picture with the Premier League trophy on his Instagram account, he captioned it ‘pure profit.’ It was an amusing clapback.

His destiny appeared to change with a roll of the dice. Arteta made a brave call to sit Zubimendi down in favour of a teenager who had yet to really play a senior game in central midfield. Lewis-Skelly repaid his manager’s faith. Lewis-Skelly, who had burst onto the scene in an unfamiliar left-back position, had repeated the trick in central midfield.

It is a quite extraordinary achievement for a teenager to break into a team the quality of Arsenal’s twice, in different positions. He has achieved it so matter-of-factly that I feel like everyone has barely noticed. This summer could also have proved complicated for Myles.

Firstly, his late season resurgence wasn’t quite enough to win a place in England’s World Cup squad. I think that was a short-sighted decision from Tuchel. However, in the September international break, MLS started three of England’s four Nations League games in central midfield.

In many ways, being spared an exhausting summer at the World Cup probably did Myles a favour in the long run. It enabled him to play a full pre-season and in central midfield too. With Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi going to the final weekend of the tournament, as well as Odegaard, Eze and Bruno going to the latter stages, he had a clear run at the position.

This put him in a strong position to start the season. However, his pre-season was complicated by two things. The signing of Bruno Guimaraes, who could have offered a further road-block to Myles’ progression. There were also strong rumours that some people in the club (!) were touting Lewis-Skelly around in a bid to raise the funds for a much-needed attacking A-lister.

While this talk was swirling around in the summer, Myles’ response was to score in a pre-season friendly against Como. What followed was even more impressive, Bruno came into the season with some fitness concerns. Lewis-Skelly’s form was such that his presence in midfield made that a total non-issue. He starred in wins at Villa Park and at home to Chelsea.

In truth, I still don’t think Bruno has done enough to firmly dislodge Myles from the role of Declan Rice’s midfield partner. His apprenticeship at left-back has also proved hugely useful and is helping him to pick up even more minutes. At Fleetwood, he played in both positions during the game, while he started games against Everton and Lille at left-back too.

Having a minor and a major is very useful for a young player looking to build his CV. He came on for Bruno in the Allianz last week and, in my view, outshone his more experienced, more expensive teammate. (Please don’t think I am having a dig at Bruno here, he has clearly conjured up some huge contributions this season too).

In a September interview with Men In Blazers, Lewis-Skelly talked about how he uses mindfulness techniques to deal with pressure and nerves. ‘There’s a Buddhism concept; it’s about the monkey mind. It’s practically about the restless mind, how you can jump from concern to concern.

‘So whenever I feel a type of weight, for me it’s important to bring my nervous system down and to bring stillness back to my mind, to be calm. Whether it is through breathing techniques, music or talking with other people, I just feel like it is important I always remain calm.’

It shows in his play and it shows in how he has dealt with certain situations. His re-ascension in the last six months has been very far from frictionless. Nothing has been given, pieces haven’t fallen into place. He has forced his way in and when he got the shirt, he gripped it for all its worth.

Just think how unlikely it felt in January that Lewis-Skelly would be significantly ahead of Zubimendi in the midfield pecking order before the clocks went back for winter. It takes a special player and a special character to negotiate those numerous challenges and to get into this team. He has met those challenges so firmly that we have barely even noticed them. His is a significant talent.

#1702. Arsenal right to appeal Dowman red

Let’s start with the news that Arsenal are set to appeal Max Dowman’s red card against Fleetwood on Tuesday evening. I think that’s probably the right thing to do, because had that gone to a VAR review, I think they’d have really struggled to make a compelling case that this was violent conduct.

Was it a small retaliation? Yes. Did it meet the threshold for violent conduct? Not for me. As laid out in the rules of the game, it is defined thus: Violent conduct is when a player uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball, or against a team-mate, team official, match official, spectator or any other person, regardless of whether contact is made.

So, on that basis I think Arsenal are right to appeal. They might cite other incidents to make their case. Perhaps the fact Cole Palmer received just a yellow card in Chelsea’s last game against Sp*rs for what was a much more violent action against Mateus Fernandes. Imagine if we even used one of our own players, demonstrating how Bruno Guimaraes was allowed to forearm smash Jorginho in the side of the head, but didn’t get sent off because he didn’t use his arm like a weapon (or something).

Mikel Arteta is a man who, just last week, ‘joked’ he had a collection of images to show other managers outside their techincal area 36 times in ten minutes. If you don’t think he can’t dig up a few more examples of players getting away with violent conduct, you haven’t been paying attention. Whether it’s going to be sufficient to have the red card overturned is another thing, but at the very least we should see a reduction in what is, as it stands, a three match ban. I think the red was very, very, very harsh, but to miss three games because of that is absurd and unfair, so I think we’re right to appeal.

Once again though, there’s a conversation to be had about the punishments for red cards, and how it’s kind of ridiculous that every act of violent conduct = a three game ban. Some acts are more violent than others, some really do endanger the safety of an opponent, and yet they’re all treated the same. It’s never made sense to me, and I don’t really understand how there isn’t a disciplinary panel that assesses each sending off and applies the ban after the fact based on the seriousness of the incident.

Despite his frustration in the moment, I’m sure the manager’s view of Dowman’s behaviour might well have softened on watching the replays. In the heat of the moment part of it, I’m sure, is that we currently have Christos Tzolis and Bukayo Saka sidelined while Noni Madueke missed out on the midweek game to protect an ankle knock. So, we’re very light in the wide areas right now, and while the root cause of that might lie more at the door of the Sporting Director, he would have wanted Dowman available this weekend for the trip to Anfield.

I still think Arteta’s reaction was poor, but football is a game of opinions. I’ve seen some suggest if Max is gonna play with the big boys, he’s got to be treated as an equal. Perhaps that’s fair enough, but I’ve never seen Arteta react like that to a senior player being sent off, and we’ve had plenty of red cards during his tenure. You could argue that his age is why it’s different, that we all need to learn lessons when we’re younger in ways that differ from when we’re more grown up.

For me though, as talented as he is and as excited as we are about what he might become, it’s too easy to lose sight of the fact he is just 16, and that does make it different. It was so interesting that last week, after Bukayo Saka got injured against Bayern, there were myriad conversations about how Arteta was culpable to some extent because of how much he asked of the player since his breakthrough. And in the same breath, many of the same people were saying ‘It’s time for Dowman!’. I find it a little hard to square that circle. Do you actually care about the welfare of a young player or not?

I think Arteta has generally been rightly protective of Max. He knows that exposure at this age is something he and his staff have to consider for all kinds of reasons, and his playing time this season has been limited. In this instance though, regardless of the fact it’s just a few sharp words on the sideline, he’s made this a bigger issue than it should have been, with Dowman firmly in the spotlight, and I’ll be curious to see how he addresses it in his pre-Liverpool press conference tomorrow.
